item.content:encoded:
The World Health Organization (WHO) is inviting qualified urban health professionals, policymakers, city practitioners, and experienced facilitators of multi-sectoral processes to apply for its 2nd WHO Training on the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Kit.

This four-week online training is designed to strengthen the ability of professionals and cross-sectoral teams to understand, assess, and respond to urban health challenges through collaborative approaches. The programme focuses on the practical use of the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit, which helps policymakers and practitioners identify existing capacities, recognize gaps, develop response strategies, and work collaboratively across different sectors to improve health and wellbeing in cities.

The training will take place online through four sessions scheduled for 17 September, 24 September, 1 October and 8 October 2026. Each session will run for two hours from 14:00 to 16:00 CET, with participants also expected to dedicate additional time to preparation and assignments.

According to the WHO announcement, the training is intended for professionals who are actively involved in shaping urban environments, public policy, health, infrastructure, transport, housing, climate resilience, food systems, security, economic development and other areas that influence the health and wellbeing of urban populations.

About the WHO Urban Health Capacity Training

Urbanization is transforming the way people live, work and access essential services. As cities continue to grow, policymakers and practitioners face increasingly complex challenges involving public health, infrastructure, climate change, inequality, housing, transport, food systems, governance and access to basic services.

The WHO’s Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit is designed to help professionals respond to these interconnected challenges by taking a whole-of-city and intersectoral approach.

The resource recognizes that urban health cannot be addressed by the health sector alone. Decisions involving transportation, urban planning, housing, infrastructure, environmental management, economic development, food systems, governance and public safety can all have direct or indirect effects on population health.

The training therefore provides participants with the knowledge and practical skills needed to assess the capacities available within urban systems, identify weaknesses and strengths, and develop strategies for addressing capacity gaps.

Why Urban Health Capacity Building Matters

Rapid urbanization, climate change and socio-economic inequalities are creating increasingly complex pressures on cities.

Urban health challenges often involve several sectors at the same time. For example, improving health outcomes in a city may require coordinated action involving public health authorities, transport planners, housing agencies, environmental institutions, local government, community organizations and economic actors.

The WHO resource kit is intended to support this kind of collaboration.

It can help professionals working to influence areas such as:

  • Transportation and mobility
  • Urban planning
  • Housing and real estate development
  • Infrastructure and basic services
  • Public health
  • Governance
  • Food systems and nutrition
  • Climate resilience
  • Environmental management
  • Safety and security
  • Economy and livelihoods
  • Community participation

By identifying what capacities already exist and where gaps remain, practitioners can develop more targeted and practical responses to urban challenges.

The training will therefore be particularly relevant to professionals who are seeking to connect health considerations with broader urban development policies and interventions.

Who Should Apply for the WHO Urban Health Training?

The WHO has identified two main categories of applicants for the 2026 training.

1. Cross-Sectoral Teams of Urban Practitioners

The WHO is encouraging applications from teams of three to four individuals who share a common urban health goal.

A qualifying team should include professionals from at least two different sectors or organizations. This is intended to ensure that participants bring different perspectives and areas of expertise to the training.

Potential sectors may include:

  • Built environment and infrastructure
  • Health and social services
  • Environment and climate resilience
  • Safety and security
  • Food systems and nutrition
  • Economy and employment
  • Transportation
  • Urban planning
  • Housing
  • Other sectors that influence urban health

The team members may come from public or private institutions, including:

  • Local government agencies
  • National government agencies
  • Civil society organizations
  • Other relevant institutions

Teams that already have a shared urban health objective are particularly well suited to the programme because they can apply the Resource Kit collaboratively to a real-world urban challenge.

2. Individual Facilitators of Intersectoral Processes

Individual applicants can also apply if they have significant experience facilitating multi-sectoral processes.

The WHO is looking for professionals who have experience with activities such as:

  • Joint planning exercises
  • Stakeholder dialogues
  • Inter-agency collaborations
  • Multi-sectoral projects
  • Cross-sectoral coordination
  • Urban health planning processes

Individual applicants should also have a close working relationship with a local government.

They may work within:

  • Local government
  • Academia
  • Private organizations
  • Civil society organizations

However, the organization should have a primary focus on improving urban living conditions and health where applicable.

Approximately 50 participants are expected to take part in the training.

WHO Urban Health Training Eligibility Requirements

Applicants are expected to meet several professional and academic requirements.

Professional Background

The training is open to professionals working in policy-making and city-level practice, particularly those whose work influences urban health.

Relevant professionals may include those working in:

  • Public health policy
  • Urban policy
  • Transport and mobility
  • Housing and real estate
  • Infrastructure and services
  • Economy and livelihoods
  • Security and justice
  • Urban development
  • Other fields connected to urban health

Applicants should have experience working in multi-sectoral environments and facilitating or participating in multi-sectoral processes.

Academic Qualifications

Applicants should have:

  • A bachelor’s-level university degree; and
  • At least five years of professional experience, or three years of experience combined with an advanced degree.

Applicants should also demonstrate an interest in or experience with urban health and capacity building.

Language Requirement

Participants must have an excellent command of English, as English is the working language of the training.

Preference for Cross-Sectoral Teams

The WHO states that preference will be given to teams.

To qualify as a team, the application group should consist of three to four individuals who meet the stated eligibility requirements and come from at least two different sectors or organizations.

For example, a team could combine professionals from the following:

  • Public health and transportation
  • Local government and civil society
  • Urban planning and environmental management
  • Health and infrastructure
  • Food systems and nutrition and local government

The purpose of this arrangement is to encourage participants to apply the training through different professional perspectives and strengthen collaboration between sectors.

What Will Participants Learn?

The training will focus on developing practical competencies that can be applied to real urban health challenges.

Participants will learn how to use the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit to understand their existing capacities, identify weaknesses and develop appropriate strategies.

Key learning areas include:

1. Informed Decision-Making, Monitoring and Evaluation

Participants will learn how evidence and data can support urban health policies and decision-making.

This component emphasizes the importance of using reliable information to understand urban challenges, monitor interventions and evaluate whether policies and programmes are achieving their intended outcomes.

2. Policy Coherence and Multi-Sectoral Governance

Urban health challenges frequently cross institutional and sectoral boundaries.

The training will therefore examine ways of strengthening governance structures and improving collaboration among sectors so that policies and interventions work toward shared objectives rather than operating in isolation.

3. Sustainable Financing and Resource Mobilization

Participants will also explore ways of identifying financing mechanisms and strategic investments that can support urban health initiatives.

This is particularly important because urban health interventions often require sustained resources, coordination and investment across multiple institutions.

4. Partnerships and Participation

The programme will emphasize stakeholder engagement and partnerships.

Participants will learn about approaches for bringing different partners and stakeholders into urban health initiatives and strengthening participation in decision-making and implementation.

Key Competencies Participants Will Develop

By the end of the training, participants are expected to strengthen their ability to:

  • Conduct urban health capacity assessments using the Resource Kit.
  • Identify critical strengths and capacity gaps within urban systems.
  • Develop actionable response strategies suited to local circumstances.
  • Work effectively across different sectors to address urban health challenges.
  • Use participatory approaches to strengthen urban governance.
  • Integrate health equity considerations into urban policies and interventions.

These competencies are intended to help participants move beyond identifying urban health problems toward developing practical, coordinated and locally appropriate responses.

Main Objective of the Training

The primary objective of the WHO training is to develop awareness of the cross-disciplinary capacities required for effective urban health action and policy-making.

Particular emphasis will be placed on areas such as:

  • Data analysis
  • Policy coherence
  • Community engagement
  • Financing strategies
  • Cross-sectoral collaboration
  • Urban governance

The training also aims to build a cohort of professionals capable of applying the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit in their respective settings.

Additional Objectives

Beyond the primary objective, the programme seeks to:

  1. Build a professional cohort skilled in applying the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit.
  2. Strengthen participants’ ability to identify, assess and address urban health challenges using a capacity-based approach.
  3. Encourage collaboration among professionals working in urban health.
  4. Facilitate peer-to-peer learning and knowledge exchange.
  5. Support the development of strategic responses to urban health challenges.

These objectives make the programme relevant not only for individual professional development but also for organizations seeking to improve their approaches to urban health and cross-sectoral planning.

Training Format and Schedule

The WHO training will be delivered entirely online.

The programme consists of four online sessions, each lasting two hours.

The scheduled sessions are:

  • 17 September 2026
  • 24 September 2026
  • 1 October 2026
  • 8 October 2026

Each session will take place from 14:00 to 16:00 CET.

In addition to the live sessions, participants should expect approximately 4 to 6 hours of offline preparation and assignment work.

Online Delivery Through Zoom

The programme will be delivered through Zoom and will combine different learning approaches, including:

  • Expert presentations
  • Breakout discussions
  • Interactive exercises
  • Practical application of the Resource Kit
  • Case studies
  • Collaborative exercises

Participants will therefore be expected to take an active role rather than simply attend lectures.

Participation and Attendance Requirements

Successful applicants will be expected to actively participate throughout the programme.

The WHO requires participants to:

  • Attend 100% of the training sessions.
  • Participate actively in the sessions.
  • Complete assigned preparation and other required assignments.
  • Engage in collaborative and interactive exercises.

Participants who meet the attendance and engagement requirements will receive a certificate of completion.

What Do Applicants Need to Submit?

Applicants must prepare three main components for their application.

1. Letter of Interest

Applicants must submit a letter of interest of no more than 500 words.

The letter should explain:

  • The applicant’s relevant professional experience.
  • Their motivation for participating in the training.
  • Their interest in applying the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit.

Applicants should use the letter to demonstrate how their professional background aligns with the objectives of the programme.

2. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must provide an up-to-date CV highlighting their academic qualifications, professional experience and relevant work in urban health, multi-sectoral collaboration, policy-making, facilitation or related areas.

The CV should clearly demonstrate that the applicant meets the programme’s professional and academic requirements.

3. Personal Video Statement

Applicants are required to submit a personal video statement of no more than five minutes.

The video must respond to the question:

Why do you want to participate in this training and apply the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit?

Applicants must also answer two of the scenario-based questions provided by the WHO.

Scenario Questions for the Video Statement

Applicants can choose two of the following scenarios.

Scenario 1: Urban Health Multi-Sectoral Project

Applicants may describe an urban health multi-sectoral project they have worked on.

They should explain:

  • The objective of the project.
  • Who was involved.
  • How the project was implemented.

This question provides an opportunity to demonstrate practical experience in working across sectors.

Scenario 2: Multi-Sectoral Coordination Challenge

Applicants may describe a challenge they encountered while facilitating or coordinating a multi-sectoral project.

They should explain:

  • What the challenge was.
  • Who was involved.
  • How they addressed the challenge.
  • How the issue was ultimately resolved.

This allows applicants to demonstrate problem-solving, coordination, communication and facilitation skills.

Scenario 3: Relevant Strengths and Skills

Applicants can alternatively discuss their strengths and skills in relation to the objectives of the training.

They should explain:

  • Which skills they consider critical for conducting an urban health capacities assessment and response exercise.
  • How they developed those skills.
  • Examples of situations where they have applied those skills.

Applicants should use concrete professional examples wherever possible.

How to Apply for the WHO Urban Health Training

Applicants are required to submit their:

  • Letter of interest
  • CV
  • Personal video statement

The application should be sent by email to the WHO at urbanhealth@who.int, with copies to obandof@who.int and macauleym@who.int.

The required email subject line is:

“Urban health capacities Training Application”

Applicants should ensure that all required materials are included before submitting their application.

APPLY HERE

WHO Urban Health Training Deadline

There is an important deadline discrepancy in the WHO announcement that applicants should be aware of.

The announcement headline states:

Deadline for submissions: 4 September 2026.

However, the detailed submission instructions state that applications should be submitted by 28 August 2026.

Because the detailed submission instructions provide the earlier date, applicants should treat 28 August 2026 as the safer deadline and submit as soon as possible rather than waiting for 4 September.

Is the WHO Training Free?

Yes. The WHO states that participation in the training is free.

The working language of the programme is English.

Applicants should nevertheless take into account any personal costs associated with internet access, equipment and participation in the online sessions, as the source does not specify financial support for such expenses.

Countries and Regions Eligible to Apply

The WHO announcement does not specify a restricted list of eligible countries or a particular continent from which applicants must originate.

The opportunity is therefore presented as an international professional training opportunity for eligible professionals, with the WHO specifically stating that women and professionals from low- and middle-income countries are especially encouraged to apply.

The emphasis on low- and middle-income countries makes the opportunity particularly relevant to professionals working in developing urban environments where rapid urbanization, climate pressures, infrastructure gaps and socio-economic inequalities can create complex health challenges.

Who Is Most Likely to Benefit From This Training?

The programme could be particularly valuable for professionals whose work involves influencing urban policies, programmes or systems.

Potential applicants include:

  • Urban health professionals
  • Public health policymakers
  • City practitioners
  • Local government officials
  • Urban planners
  • Transport and mobility professionals
  • Housing and infrastructure practitioners
  • Environmental and climate resilience professionals
  • Food systems and nutrition professionals
  • Social service professionals
  • Security and justice practitioners
  • Economic development professionals
  • Civil society practitioners
  • Academics working on urban health
  • Professionals facilitating multi-sectoral partnerships
  • Professionals involved in inter-agency collaboration
  • Practitioners working to improve urban living conditions

The strongest applicants are likely to be those who can demonstrate both professional experience and an ability to work collaboratively across sectors.

Why This Opportunity Could Be Valuable for Professionals

The WHO training offers participants an opportunity to strengthen their understanding of how different urban systems interact with health.

Rather than approaching urban health as the responsibility of one institution or profession, the programme promotes a collaborative model in which multiple sectors contribute to healthier urban environments.

Participants can potentially benefit from:

  • Developing practical urban health assessment skills.
  • Learning how to identify capacity gaps and existing strengths.
  • Improving multi-sectoral coordination skills.
  • Strengthening policy and governance approaches.
  • Learning about sustainable financing and resource mobilization.
  • Developing stakeholder engagement and participation skills.
  • Applying evidence and data to urban health decision-making.
  • Learning through case studies and collaborative exercises.
  • Connecting with other professionals working in urban health.
  • Receiving a certificate of completion after meeting the programme requirements.

The programme’s emphasis on practical application means that participants can potentially use the Resource Kit within their own professional and urban contexts after completing the training.

Visit HERE for more information about the WHO 2026 Urban Health Training.

How Applicants Can Prepare a Strong Application

Although the WHO announcement does not provide a ranking formula for applications, prospective applicants can strengthen their submissions by clearly connecting their experience to the programme’s objectives.

Applicants should consider demonstrating:

Relevant Professional Experience

Explain previous work involving urban health, city development, public policy, infrastructure, community engagement, environmental management or another field affecting urban health.

Multi-Sectoral Experience

Clearly describe experience working with people or institutions from different sectors. This is particularly important because cross-sectoral collaboration is central to the training.

Facilitation and Coordination Skills

Applicants applying as individual facilitators should emphasize experience organizing stakeholder dialogues, joint planning activities, inter-agency collaborations or other multi-sectoral processes.

A Clear Urban Health Challenge

Applicants who apply as teams should identify a specific urban health goal that the team shares. They should also demonstrate how the members’ different sectoral backgrounds contribute to addressing that goal.

Practical Examples

For the video statement, applicants should avoid relying only on general statements about their skills. The scenario questions provide an opportunity to demonstrate practical experience through specific examples, including challenges encountered, actions taken and results achieved.

Important Information for Team Applicants

Professionals interested in applying as a team should consider forming a group of three or four eligible individuals before submitting their application.

The team should:

  1. Include three to four professionals.
  2. Ensure members meet the stated eligibility criteria.
  3. Include individuals from at least two different sectors or organizations.
  4. Identify a shared urban health goal.
  5. Demonstrate experience or interest in addressing urban health challenges.
  6. Prepare an application that communicates how the team could benefit from applying the Resource Kit together.

Because preference is given to teams, eligible professionals who already collaborate across sectors may wish to consider a team application.

Key Details at a Glance

Opportunity: 2nd WHO Training on Urban Health Capacity Assessment and Response Kit

Organiser: World Health Organization

Category: Training / Professional Development Opportunity

Format: Online

Platform: Zoom

Duration: Four weeks

Training dates: 17 September, 24 September, 1 October and 8 October 2026

Session time: 14:00–16:00 CET

Session length: Two hours per session

Additional commitment: Approximately 4–6 hours for offline preparation and assignments

Expected participants: Approximately 50

Cost: Free

Working language: English

Academic requirement: Bachelor’s-level university degree

Experience requirement: At least five years of professional experience, or three years plus an advanced degree

Additional experience: Multi-sectoral work and facilitation, plus demonstrated interest or experience in urban health and capacity building

Team option: Three to four people from at least two sectors or organizations

Application documents: Letter of interest, CV, and personal video statement

Letter limit: Maximum 500 words

Video limit: Maximum five minutes

Certificate: Awarded to participants who meet attendance and engagement requirements

Priority encouragement: Women and professionals from low- and middle-income countries

Deadline stated in announcement header: 4 September 2026

Deadline stated in detailed submission instructions: 28 August 2026

Conclusion

The WHO 2026 Urban Health Capacity Assessment and Response Kit Training presents an opportunity for professionals and cross-sectoral teams to strengthen their ability to address the increasingly complex health challenges associated with urbanization.

The programme recognizes that healthier cities require cooperation across multiple areas, including health, transportation, housing, infrastructure, climate resilience, food systems, governance, economic development and community participation. Through the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit, participants will learn how to assess existing capacities, identify gaps, develop practical response strategies and strengthen collaboration across sectors.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to professionals with experience in urban development, public policy, public health, local government and multisectoral facilitation. Teams of three to four professionals from different sectors are encouraged, while experienced individual facilitators with strong local government connections can also apply.

Since the source contains different dates for the submission deadline, prospective applicants should exercise caution and follow the earlier 28 August 2026 deadline stated in the detailed submission instructions unless the WHO confirms otherwise.

For professionals seeking to strengthen their expertise in urban health, intersectoral collaboration and evidence-based urban policy, this free WHO training offers an opportunity to gain practical skills, engage with peers and apply a structured resource to real-world urban health challenges.

For more global Training opportunities, visit OFY HERE.

Apply for 15 ACT-PREP PhD and 10 postdoctoral research fellowships in clinical trials and epidemic preparedness. Review funding, eligibility, research themes, documents, partner universities and September 2026 deadlines.

Applications are open for 25 ACT-PREP research fellowships designed to strengthen Africa’s capacity in clinical trials, infectious-disease surveillance, epidemic preparedness and emergency response.

The current call offers:

  • 15 PhD research fellowships.
  • 10 postdoctoral research fellowships.

The opportunities are available to eligible nationals of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Senegal, Somalia, South Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda. Applicants must propose research connected to clinical trials or epidemic preparedness and response while meeting the academic and institutional requirements of their selected fellowship category.

The programme provides tuition support, monthly stipends, research funding, mentorship, specialized training, access to research sites and datasets, and professional networking opportunities. The precise package depends on whether the candidate applies under PhD Round 1, PhD Round 2 or the postdoctoral category.

The official announcement from Makerere University was published on August 14, 2026.

ACT-PREP Research Fellowships at a Glance

Programme detail Information
Programme ACT-PREP
Available opportunities 15 PhD and 10 postdoctoral positions
Main fields Clinical trials and epidemic preparedness and response research
Funding programme HORIZON-JU-GH-EDCTP3
PhD funding period Up to three years
Postdoctoral funding period Up to 12 months
PhD Round 1 deadline September 15, 2026
PhD Round 2 deadline September 30, 2026
Postdoctoral deadline September 30, 2026
Eligible nationalities DRC, Rwanda, Senegal, Somalia, South Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda
Application languages English or French
Application method Submission by email
Number of priority themes Seven
Female applicants Strongly encouraged
Application fee No application fee is stated

What Is ACT-PREP?

ACT-PREP is a multi-country research and capacity-strengthening initiative focused on improving Africa’s preparedness for infectious-disease outbreaks and other public-health emergencies.

The project seeks to strengthen the continent’s ability to conduct timely, ethical and scientifically rigorous clinical research before and during disease outbreaks. It focuses on institutionalizing clinical-trial preparedness within national public-health systems instead of treating research as a separate activity that begins only after an emergency occurs.

According to the official Global Health EDCTP3 project profile, ACT-PREP runs from June 1, 2026, to May 31, 2031. The wider project has been awarded approximately €12.75 million in Global Health EDCTP3 funding.

This amount represents funding for the overall multi-year ACT-PREP project. It is not the individual amount payable to each fellow.

The initiative aims to build clinical research and outbreak-response capacity through:

  • PhD and postdoctoral research support.
  • Short- and long-term professional training.
  • Mentorship programmes.
  • Research exchanges.
  • Access to real-world datasets.
  • Practical training at clinical-trial and surveillance sites.
  • Training for clinical-trial monitors.
  • Strengthening of ethics and regulatory-review systems.
  • Improved surveillance and health-information systems.
  • Laboratory and data-management upgrades.
  • Standardized outbreak-research protocols.
  • Community engagement.
  • Institutional and regional research partnerships.

The wider project intends to train more than 700 senior researchers in advanced methods, support 15 PhD students and 10 postdoctoral researchers, and train an additional 80 clinical-trial monitors.

Why the ACT-PREP Programme Is Needed

Africa continues to experience a substantial burden of infectious diseases and public-health emergencies.

The official call reports that the African region recorded 2,234 acute public-health events between 2001 and 2022. Approximately 92% were infectious-disease events, while zoonotic outbreaks increased substantially during the period.

Recent outbreaks have repeatedly revealed structural limitations, including:

  • Fragmented disease-surveillance systems.
  • Weak integration of human, animal and environmental health information.
  • Delayed laboratory confirmation.
  • Limited diagnostic infrastructure.
  • Slow deployment of outbreak research.
  • Inadequate readiness to launch clinical trials during emergencies.
  • Limited research coordination across countries.
  • Delays in ethics and regulatory review.
  • Insufficient pharmacovigilance capacity.
  • Weak integration of research into emergency-response systems.

ACT-PREP seeks to address these gaps by strengthening research, surveillance, ethics, diagnostics, pharmacovigilance, regulation and policy across Africa’s emergency preparedness and response ecosystem.

Diseases and Public-Health Areas Covered

ACT-PREP has a broad infectious-disease and health-security mandate. Its wider programme focuses particularly on:

  • HIV and AIDS.
  • Malaria.
  • Tuberculosis.
  • Neglected tropical diseases.
  • Emerging infectious diseases.
  • Re-emerging infectious diseases.
  • Epidemic-prone pathogens.
  • Zoonotic diseases.
  • Outbreak-related clinical research.

Applicants should ensure that their proposed research is relevant to the programme’s mandate and to an EDCTP-priority disease or health-security challenge.

Seven ACT-PREP Priority Research Themes

Applicants must align their proposed work with at least one of the following research themes:

1. Clinical Trials and Trial Readiness

This theme can include work on:

  • Clinical-trial design and implementation.
  • Trial-site preparedness.
  • Rapid activation of trials during outbreaks.
  • Clinical research quality systems.
  • Participant recruitment and retention.
  • Trial-monitoring approaches.
  • Community engagement in clinical research.
  • Standardized outbreak-trial protocols.
  • Trial data quality and management.

2. Disease Surveillance, Modelling and Artificial Intelligence

Relevant research may address:

  • Early-warning systems.
  • Disease forecasting.
  • Epidemiological modelling.
  • Digital surveillance.
  • Artificial intelligence for outbreak detection.
  • Integration of surveillance information.
  • Analysis of routine health data.
  • Predictive analytics.
  • Data visualization for emergency response.
  • Integration with health-information systems such as DHIS2.

3. Ethics and Regulatory Science

This area may include:

  • Ethics-review procedures during outbreaks.
  • Regulatory preparedness.
  • Rapid but responsible research review.
  • Protection of research participants.
  • Digital systems for ethics and regulatory authorities.
  • Regulatory coordination across countries.
  • Pharmacovigilance regulation.
  • Ethical governance of emergency research.
  • Research integrity.

4. Laboratory and Genomic Surveillance

Possible topics include:

  • Genomic sequencing.
  • Pathogen detection.
  • Diagnostic technologies.
  • Laboratory quality systems.
  • Molecular epidemiology.
  • Laboratory-network strengthening.
  • Data management for genomic surveillance.
  • Rapid diagnostic confirmation.
  • Laboratory preparedness for epidemics.

5. One Health

This theme recognizes the connection between human, animal and environmental health. Research can explore:

  • Zoonotic-disease surveillance.
  • Human-animal transmission pathways.
  • Environmental drivers of outbreaks.
  • Integrated surveillance systems.
  • Collaboration between medical, veterinary and environmental institutions.
  • Community-level disease prevention.
  • Cross-sector emergency preparedness.

6. Health-Systems Resilience

Relevant work may examine:

  • Health-system continuity during emergencies.
  • Preparedness of healthcare facilities.
  • Workforce readiness.
  • Supply chains during outbreaks.
  • Integration of research into routine public-health systems.
  • Emergency governance.
  • Community trust and engagement.
  • Equitable access to emergency interventions.

7. Epidemic Preparedness and Response

This broad area can cover:

  • National and regional preparedness.
  • Emergency-response systems.
  • Outbreak investigation.
  • Rapid research deployment.
  • Policy responses.
  • Public-health communication.
  • Emergency coordination.
  • Evaluation of preparedness plans.
  • Lessons from previous epidemics.

PhD Fellowships: Two Application Routes

ACT-PREP has created two separate PhD application rounds. Applicants must select the correct route based on whether they are already enrolled in a doctoral programme.

PhD Round 1: Currently Enrolled Doctoral Researchers

PhD Round 1 is intended for applicants who are already enrolled in a relevant doctoral programme at an ACT-PREP partner university.

Applicants must already be conducting or developing doctoral research under one of the seven ACT-PREP priority themes.

PhD Round 1 Eligibility

Applicants should:

  • Be nationals of an eligible ACT-PREP country.
  • Hold a relevant master’s degree or equivalent qualification.
  • Have an academic background in health, biomedical sciences, public health or a related discipline.
  • Be currently enrolled in a relevant doctoral programme at an ACT-PREP partner university.
  • Propose research aligned with an ACT-PREP priority theme.
  • Obtain formal endorsement from their home institution.
  • Provide two suitable referees.
  • Submit every required document before the closing date.
  • Commit to research quality, integrity and timely completion.

PhD Round 1 Duration

Fellows are expected to complete their doctoral programme within three years.

A justified no-cost extension may be considered under applicable university policies and approval procedures. Such an extension would not automatically provide additional fellowship funding.

PhD Round 1 Financial and Academic Support

The package may include:

  • Partial or full tuition and university fees.
  • A monthly stipend.
  • A one-time research or clinical-trial grant.
  • Mentorship from ACT-PREP specialists.
  • Core training courses.
  • Specialized courses connected to the research theme.
  • Access to consortium trial sites.
  • Access to relevant datasets.
  • Participation in research and mentorship networks.
  • Access to alumni opportunities.

The call does not state the monetary value of the monthly stipend or one-time research grant.

PhD Round 1 Deadline

September 15, 2026

PhD Round 2: Applicants Seeking Doctoral Enrolment

PhD Round 2 is intended for candidates who are not necessarily enrolled in a doctoral programme but are eligible and willing to register at an ACT-PREP partner university.

These applicants must commit to completing their doctoral training within three years.

PhD Round 2 Eligibility

Applicants should:

  • Be nationals of an ACT-PREP partner country.
  • Hold a relevant master’s degree or equivalent.
  • Have a suitable academic background in health, biomedical sciences, public health or a related field.
  • Be eligible to register for a relevant doctoral programme at an ACT-PREP partner university.
  • Propose work under one of the seven priority themes.
  • Secure institutional endorsement.
  • Identify an appropriate host institution and mentor.
  • Provide two referees.
  • Commit to completing doctoral training within three years.

Applicants affiliated with an ACT-PREP institution, including eligible junior researchers, will receive priority consideration.

PhD Round 2 Support

The fellowship may provide:

  • Tuition and university fees.
  • A monthly stipend.
  • A one-time research or clinical-trial grant.
  • Mentorship from ACT-PREP experts.
  • Core and specialized training courses.
  • Access to research sites and datasets.
  • Professional networking.
  • Alumni and mentorship opportunities.

The fellowship can be supported for up to three years, subject to programme and institutional requirements.

PhD Round 2 Deadline

September 30, 2026

Postdoctoral Research Fellowships

The ten postdoctoral positions are designed to help early-career African researchers develop independent research leadership in clinical trials and epidemic preparedness.

Selected researchers will join ongoing ACT-PREP research activities while developing and leading their own research outputs.

Their work must either:

  • Integrate appropriate clinical-trial methodologies; or
  • Address a substantive epidemic preparedness and response topic.

Postdoctoral researchers will be expected to uphold high standards of research quality, ethics and integrity.

Postdoctoral Eligibility

Applicants must:

  • Be nationals of an eligible ACT-PREP country.
  • Hold a PhD in a relevant health, biomedical or related field.
  • Have obtained the PhD within the past five years.
  • Demonstrate a research record appropriate to their postdoctoral career stage.
  • Propose research aligned with an ACT-PREP priority theme.
  • Confirm an appropriate host institution.
  • Obtain endorsement from the home or host institution.
  • Identify a suitable mentor.
  • Provide two referees.
  • Demonstrate potential for research leadership and scientific independence.
  • Submit a complete application before the deadline.

Postdoctoral Support

Selected postdoctoral researchers may receive:

  • A mentored position at a consortium partner institution.
  • A monthly stipend.
  • Research support.
  • Mobility support.
  • Funding for up to 12 months.
  • Training in scientific writing.
  • Training in research leadership.
  • Training in grant administration.
  • Specialized methodological training.
  • Exposure to modelling, bioinformatics and real-world evidence methods.
  • Support to publish research.
  • Support to present findings at conferences.
  • Guidance on securing follow-on research funding.
  • Mentorship from local and international experts.

The call does not specify the stipend, research-support or mobility-support amounts.

Postdoctoral Deadline

September 30, 2026

Eligible ACT-PREP Countries

Applicants must be nationals of one of the following seven countries:

  • Democratic Republic of the Congo.
  • Rwanda.
  • Senegal.
  • Somalia.
  • South Sudan.
  • Tanzania.
  • Uganda.

Citizenship or nationality is required. Residence in one of these countries without holding an eligible nationality may not satisfy the requirement.

ACT-PREP Partner Universities

The PhD opportunities are connected to the following universities:

  1. Makerere University, Uganda.
  2. Somali National University, Somalia.
  3. Université de Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo.
  4. Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences, Tanzania.
  5. University of Global Health Equity, Rwanda.
  6. Université Cheikh Anta Diop, Senegal.
  7. University of Juba, South Sudan.

PhD Round 1 applicants must already be enrolled at a relevant ACT-PREP partner university. Round 2 applicants must be eligible to register at a partner university.

Postdoctoral applicants must confirm an appropriate host institution and obtain the required institutional endorsement.

Application Languages

Applications may be prepared in:

  • English; or
  • French.

French-language applications are accepted, particularly from applicants connected to francophone ACT-PREP institutions, including Université de Kinshasa and Université Cheikh Anta Diop.

Applicants should use one language consistently and ensure that all documents are clear, professionally written and complete.

Required Application Documents

Applicants should submit a complete application package containing the following:

1. Completed Application Form

Applicants must complete Document D from the official application package.

The form requests:

  • Full name.
  • Sex or gender.
  • Nationality.
  • Date of birth.
  • Email address.
  • Telephone number.
  • Current position.
  • Current institution.
  • Nominating or home institution.
  • Academic qualifications.
  • Proposed research title.
  • Selected ACT-PREP research theme.
  • Proposed host institution.
  • Proposed mentor or mentors.
  • Signed declaration.

2. Academic Documents

Applicants should provide copies of relevant:

  • Degrees.
  • Academic certificates.
  • Transcripts where required.
  • Proof of current doctoral enrolment for Round 1.
  • Evidence of eligibility for doctoral registration for Round 2.
  • Proof of PhD completion date for postdoctoral applicants.

3. Updated Curriculum Vitae

The CV should clearly present:

  • Education.
  • Research experience.
  • Employment history.
  • Research projects.
  • Technical and analytical skills.
  • Research methods.
  • Conference participation.
  • Professional affiliations.
  • Awards or recognition.
  • Relevant training.
  • Publications.

Postdoctoral applicants should include a complete or appropriately selected publication list.

4. Research Concept Note

Applicants must prepare a research concept of approximately two to three pages.

It should include:

  • Working research title.
  • Selected ACT-PREP priority theme.
  • Background and rationale.
  • Research problem.
  • Objectives.
  • Proposed methodology.
  • Expected results or contributions.
  • Relevance to clinical trials or epidemic preparedness.
  • Alignment with an EDCTP-priority disease.
  • Implementation work plan.
  • Proposed host institution.
  • Proposed mentor or supervisory arrangement.
  • Expected contribution to African research capacity.

The work plan must be realistic for the fellowship duration. PhD applicants should design work that can be completed within three years, while postdoctoral candidates should present a plan achievable within 12 months.

5. Motivation Letter

The motivation letter should explain:

  • Why the applicant is interested in ACT-PREP.
  • How the opportunity relates to the applicant’s career.
  • The applicant’s relevant academic and research experience.
  • Why the selected research theme is important.
  • How the applicant will contribute to the consortium.
  • The applicant’s commitment to research quality and integrity.
  • How the applicant intends to strengthen research and epidemic preparedness in Africa.
  • The applicant’s intention to remain connected to and contribute to the region.

6. Institutional Endorsement Letter

An institutional endorsement or nomination letter is mandatory for both PhD and postdoctoral applicants.

It should be prepared on the nominating institution’s official letterhead and confirm:

  • The candidate’s status as a staff member, registered researcher or person eligible to enrol.
  • The institution’s formal support for the application.
  • Alignment of the proposed work with institutional priorities.
  • Willingness to host and support the fellow.
  • Availability of mentorship.
  • Support for enrolment where applicable.
  • Permission to participate in ACT-PREP training and research activities.
  • Institutional support throughout the fellowship period.

7. Two References

Applicants must identify two referees. The application checklist also requires two reference letters.

Referees should comment on:

  • How long they have known the applicant.
  • The capacity in which they know the applicant.
  • The applicant’s research ability.
  • Research independence.
  • Suitability for the fellowship.
  • Potential for research leadership.
  • Likelihood of timely completion.
  • Motivation.
  • Integrity.
  • Teamwork.

The official guidance instructs referees to submit their recommendations directly to the recruitment email by the applicable deadline. Applicants should therefore contact referees early and confirm that their letters have been sent.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted electronically by email.

Primary Submission Address

recruitment@act-prep.org

Addresses to Copy

actprep@musph.ac.ug
noahzyah@gmail.com

Applicants should attach all required documents and clearly identify whether they are applying for:

  • PhD Round 1.
  • PhD Round 2.
  • Postdoctoral Fellowship.

Although the call does not prescribe a mandatory email subject, candidates should use a clear subject that identifies the fellowship category and their full name.

Applicants should use the forms and templates included in the official application package.

Application Deadlines

Fellowship route Deadline
PhD Round 1 September 15, 2026
PhD Round 2 September 30, 2026
Postdoctoral Fellowship September 30, 2026

The announcement does not specify a closing time or time zone. Applicants should submit well before the relevant date and obtain confirmation that the application has been received.

Selection Process

Applications will undergo a competitive, multi-stage selection process.

Stage 1: Application Screening

The selection team will verify:

  • Completeness.
  • Eligible nationality.
  • Required academic qualification.
  • Programme enrolment or registration eligibility.
  • Institutional endorsement.
  • Presence of two referees.
  • Research-theme alignment.
  • Submission by the deadline.

Incomplete or ineligible applications may not proceed.

Stage 2: Scientific Evaluation

Eligible applications will undergo scientific review.

Reviewers will assess:

  • Quality of the research concept.
  • Scientific merit.
  • Relevance.
  • Feasibility.
  • Alignment with ACT-PREP themes.
  • Alignment with EDCTP priorities.
  • Potential contribution to clinical trials or epidemic preparedness.
  • Likely scientific or public-health impact.
  • Suitability of the work plan.

Stage 3: Interviews

Shortlisted applicants will be invited to an interview to evaluate:

  • Academic and research readiness.
  • Understanding of the proposed research.
  • Motivation.
  • Communication.
  • Suitability for the fellowship.
  • Ability to complete the research within the available time.
  • Potential for research leadership.
  • Fit with the proposed host and mentor.

Stage 4: Notification

Successful candidates will receive formal notification following the selection process.

Stage 5: Fellowship Commencement

Selected candidates will receive further instructions concerning:

  • Fellowship start date.
  • University enrolment.
  • Host-institution arrangements.
  • Mentorship.
  • Financial arrangements.
  • Training requirements.
  • Onboarding.

A detailed selection schedule will be communicated to shortlisted candidates.

How Applications Will Be Scored

Eligible applications will be evaluated according to:

  • Academic record.
  • Research experience appropriate to the applicant’s career stage.
  • Quality of the proposed research.
  • Feasibility of completing the work.
  • Relevance to clinical trials or epidemic preparedness.
  • Alignment with EDCTP research priorities.
  • Research capability.
  • Potential for leadership and scientific independence.
  • Suitability of the host institution.
  • Suitability of the proposed mentor.
  • Likelihood of timely completion.
  • Quality of motivation.
  • Commitment to contribute to the region.
  • Contribution to the consortium’s equity objectives.
  • Gender balance.
  • Equitable representation across partner countries.

Where two candidates receive equivalent scores, preference may be given to the underrepresented gender and to achieving equitable representation among ACT-PREP partner countries.

Qualified women are strongly encouraged to apply.

Practical Tips for a Competitive Application

  1. Choose the correct fellowship route

    Currently enrolled doctoral researchers should apply under Round 1. Candidates seeking admission to a doctoral programme should use Round 2.

  2. Confirm nationality before applying

    The current call is restricted to nationals of the seven listed ACT-PREP countries.

  3. Secure institutional endorsement early

    The endorsement is mandatory and may require approval from senior university or institutional officials.

  4. Identify a credible host and mentor

    The strength of the host arrangement and the likelihood of timely completion are part of the selection criteria.

  5. Align the concept with one priority theme

    Avoid presenting a general public-health topic without showing its direct connection to ACT-PREP and clinical-trial or epidemic-response priorities.

  6. Develop a realistic work plan

    The project must be achievable within three years for PhD applicants and 12 months for postdoctoral applicants.

  7. Explain the regional value of the research

    Show how the work will strengthen African research systems, institutions, policy, outbreak readiness or clinical-trial capacity.

  8. Demonstrate research integrity

    Address ethical practice, responsible data management and the protection of research participants where relevant.

  9. Use measurable objectives

    Ensure that each objective can be linked to a method, output and realistic timeline.

  10. Contact referees immediately

    Reference letters must be sent directly by the referees before the deadline.

  11. Include publications where applicable

    Postdoctoral applicants should present a research record appropriate to their career stage.

  12. Submit before the final day

    Early submission provides time to correct missing documents or email-delivery problems.

Important Points to Remember

  • There are 15 PhD and 10 postdoctoral opportunities.
  • The programme is restricted to nationals of seven ACT-PREP countries.
  • PhD Round 1 is for candidates already enrolled at partner institutions.
  • PhD Round 2 is for candidates eligible to register for a relevant doctoral programme.
  • Postdoctoral applicants must have obtained their PhD within the past five years.
  • Institutional endorsement is mandatory.
  • Two referees are required.
  • Research must align with an ACT-PREP priority theme.
  • Applications can be submitted in English or French.
  • The exact stipend and research-funding amounts are not stated.
  • PhD Round 1 closes earlier than the other categories.
  • Qualified women are strongly encouraged to apply.

Conclusion

The ACT-PREP PhD and Postdoctoral Research Fellowships provide an important opportunity for African researchers to develop expertise in clinical trials, disease surveillance, artificial intelligence, ethics, regulation, laboratory science, One Health, health-systems resilience and epidemic response.

Through academic funding, stipends, research support, specialized training, mentorship and access to a multi-country research network, the programme aims to prepare a new generation of African researchers to lead high-quality research before, during and after disease outbreaks.

Applicants must select the appropriate fellowship category, establish strong alignment with one of the seven priority themes, secure institutional endorsement and prepare a focused research concept that can be completed within the specified period.

PhD Round 1 applications must be submitted by September 15, 2026, while PhD Round 2 and postdoctoral applications must be submitted by September 30, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
The Berenson Fellowship at Harvard University’s Villa I Tatti – The Harvard University Center for Italian Renaissance Studies offers an exceptional residential research opportunity for scholars whose work explores the connections between Italy and the wider world during the Renaissance.

Supported by The Lila Wallace – Reader’s Digest Fund, the fellowship is designed to encourage research into “Italy in the World” by examining the transnational exchanges, encounters, dialogues, and cultural relationships between Italy and other regions during the Renaissance, broadly understood as the period from the 14th through the 17th century.

The fellowship is particularly interested in research that moves beyond a narrowly European understanding of the Renaissance and examines Italy’s relationships with cultures and societies across regions such as Africa, the Mediterranean, Latin America, and Asia.

Selected Fellows will be based in Florence, Italy, where they will have dedicated time for research, access to Harvard’s extensive scholarly resources at I Tatti, and opportunities to participate in the intellectual life of the Center. The fellowship provides USD 5,200 per month, in addition to a relocation supplement of up to USD 1,800.

Up to four Berenson Fellowships are awarded each year, making this a highly selective opportunity for established and emerging scholars working on original research related to the Renaissance and its global connections.

What Is the Berenson Fellowship?

The Berenson Fellowship is a residential research fellowship hosted by Villa I Tatti – The Harvard University Center for Italian Renaissance Studies in Florence.

The fellowship takes its name from Bernard Berenson, an influential scholar and art historian associated with I Tatti. In his 1956 statement, “On the Future of I Tatti,” Berenson expressed a vision in which scholars would come from different parts of the world and develop a broad understanding of the Mediterranean and its surrounding regions.

The Berenson Fellowship builds on this vision by encouraging scholarship that examines the Renaissance from a geographically expansive perspective.

Rather than treating the Renaissance solely as a European phenomenon, the fellowship seeks to support research investigating the connections between Italy and other cultures and regions.

These connections may include:

  • Cultural exchanges between Italy and Africa.
  • Italy’s historical relationships with Mediterranean societies.
  • Connections between Italy and Asian cultures.
  • Transnational relationships involving Latin America.
  • Intellectual exchanges across geographical boundaries.
  • Movement of ideas, artistic traditions, texts, technologies, and people.
  • Cross-cultural interactions during the Renaissance and early modern period.
  • The influence of non-European cultures on Italian Renaissance developments.
  • Italy’s role within wider networks of the early modern world.

The fellowship therefore offers an opportunity for scholars to develop research that places the Italian Renaissance within a broader international and intercultural context.

Berenson Fellowship Research Theme: “Italy in the World”

The central theme of the fellowship is “Italy in the World.”

Applicants are expected to propose projects that address transnational dialogues between Italy and other cultures during the Renaissance.

The Renaissance is interpreted broadly for purposes of this fellowship, covering approximately the 14th to 17th centuries.

This broad chronological and geographical approach allows researchers to investigate subjects that cross conventional disciplinary and regional boundaries.

A strong project should therefore demonstrate how Italy was connected to wider intellectual, cultural, artistic, political, scientific, or social networks.

For example, research could examine:

  1. Italian artistic exchanges with other regions.
  2. Mediterranean intellectual networks.
  3. African-Italian cultural encounters.
  4. Italian relationships with Asian societies.
  5. The circulation of Renaissance texts across borders.
  6. Music and musical traditions moving between cultures.
  7. Scientific knowledge exchanged between Italy and other regions.
  8. Philosophical interactions between Italian and non-Italian thinkers.
  9. Architectural influences crossing geographical boundaries.
  10. Literary connections between Italian writers and writers from other cultures.
  11. Trade, travel, migration, and their influence on Renaissance culture.
  12. The movement of artistic techniques, manuscripts, objects, and ideas.
  13. Cross-cultural encounters involving the Mediterranean and its hinterlands.

The key consideration is that the project should contribute to a broader understanding of the Renaissance as a connected and geographically expansive historical phenomenon.

Academic Fields Supported by the Fellowship

The Berenson Fellowship welcomes scholars working across the range of disciplines supported by I Tatti.

Applicants may come from fields including:

Architecture and the Arts

Researchers can investigate architecture, painting, sculpture, visual culture, material culture, artistic exchange, and related areas.

Projects may explore how artistic ideas, styles, techniques, or objects moved between Italy and other parts of the world.

History

Historical research may examine political, social, cultural, economic, diplomatic, or intellectual relationships between Italy and other regions during the Renaissance.

Philosophy

Philosophical projects may explore intellectual exchanges, circulation of ideas, philosophical traditions, and relationships between Italian thinkers and intellectual traditions elsewhere.

Literature

Researchers may examine texts, literary movements, translation, cultural exchange, multilingual literary networks, and relationships between Italian and non-Italian literary traditions.

Music

Music scholars can investigate musical exchange, performance traditions, composers, instruments, musical theory, and the movement of music across geographical and cultural boundaries.

History of Science

Projects may investigate scientific knowledge, technologies, discoveries, instruments, scholarly networks, and intellectual exchanges linking Italy with other parts of the world.

Applicants should ensure that their proposed project clearly fits within the intellectual scope of I Tatti while addressing the fellowship’s emphasis on transnational connections.

Why the Berenson Fellowship Is a Valuable Research Opportunity

The fellowship is designed to provide scholars with something that is increasingly difficult to obtain: extended, uninterrupted time to focus primarily on research.

I Tatti emphasizes a combination of substantial scholarly resources and relatively few obligations.

Fellows can devote their time to developing their research project rather than balancing it with extensive teaching or administrative responsibilities.

The fellowship provides:

  • A residential research appointment in Florence.
  • A grant of USD 5,200 per month.
  • A relocation supplement of up to USD 1,800.
  • Access to the scholarly resources of Harvard’s I Tatti Center.
  • Access to the Biblioteca Berenson.
  • A dedicated desk or carrel in the library.
  • Opportunities to participate in the intellectual community at I Tatti.
  • Participation in selected activities organized at the Center.
  • Opportunities to attend conferences, lectures, and concerts.
  • Interaction with scholars from different countries and academic disciplines.
  • A research environment designed to minimize interruptions and obligations.

These resources can be particularly valuable for scholars preparing a major scholarly publication, completing an extensive research project, or developing research that requires access to specialized materials available in Florence.

Fellowship Duration

The Berenson Fellowship is a residential fellowship lasting either four or six months.

Applicants are asked to indicate their preferred fellowship period:

  • Fall: September through December.
  • Winter-Spring: January through June.

The exact fellowship arrangement will depend on the appointment offered.

Because the fellowship is residential, Fellows are expected to live in the Florence area and spend at least three days per week at I Tatti.

This requirement reflects the Center’s goal of creating an active scholarly community in which Fellows interact with other researchers and participate in the intellectual life of the institution.

Financial Support and Fellowship Grant

One of the major attractions of the Berenson Fellowship is its substantial financial support.

Selected Fellows receive:

Monthly Grant

The fellowship provides a grant of:

USD 5,200 per month

This provides substantial financial support during the residential research period.

Relocation Support

In addition to the monthly grant, Fellows can receive a one-time relocation supplement of up to USD 1,800.

The supplement is intended to assist with expenses associated with relocating to Florence for the fellowship.

Housing

Because the fellowship is residential, Fellows must live in the Florence area.

When possible, I Tatti will set aside an apartment for the Fellow’s use. The apartment is provided rent free, although the Fellow is responsible for utility charges.

If an I Tatti apartment is not available, the Center will provide a housing subsidy to help offset rental expenses.

This housing arrangement can significantly reduce the cost of relocating to Florence for the fellowship period.

Access to Harvard’s Scholarly Resources

Berenson Fellows enjoy the privileges available to Fellows at I Tatti.

One of the most important resources is the Biblioteca Berenson, which Fellows can use seven days a week.

This access is particularly important for scholars whose research requires specialized Renaissance materials and scholarly resources.

Fellows also have their own desk or carrel in the Library.

However, Term Fellows do not receive a separate private office or study.

The research environment is therefore centered around the library and broader scholarly community of I Tatti.

Participation in the I Tatti Intellectual Community

Although Fellows receive substantial freedom to focus on their research, the fellowship is not intended to be an isolated research experience.

Selected activities at I Tatti are reserved for Fellows, and Fellows are expected to become part of the wider scholarly community.

They are expected to participate in activities such as:

  • Conferences.
  • Academic lectures.
  • Concerts.
  • Scholarly gatherings.
  • Other intellectual activities organized by I Tatti.

This community-oriented approach allows researchers to exchange ideas with scholars working across different disciplines and geographical areas.

For applicants interested in building international academic networks, this aspect of the fellowship can be particularly valuable.

Berenson Fellowship Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must satisfy several important eligibility requirements.

PhD Requirement

At the time of application, candidates must already hold a PhD.

Applicants will be required to upload a scan of their PhD certificate as part of the application process.

This means the fellowship is not intended for doctoral students who are still completing their first PhD.

Applicants Cannot Be Pursuing a Second PhD

Candidates may not be working on a second PhD at the time of application.

This requirement should be carefully considered by applicants who have completed one doctoral degree but are enrolled in another doctoral programme.

Research Project Requirement

Applicants must apply with a specific research project.

The proposed project should align with the Berenson Fellowship’s central focus on Italy in the World and the transnational relationships between Italy and other cultures during the Renaissance.

The proposed research can form part of a larger scholarly project.

However, applicants must be able to demonstrate that the specific project presented in the application is sufficiently developed and appropriate for the fellowship period.

Full-Time Research Commitment

Successful Fellows are expected to work solely on the project for which they applied.

They are not permitted to simultaneously work on editing other book or article projects.

This is an important condition because the fellowship is designed to provide uninterrupted time for a particular research project.

Applicants should therefore select a project that can benefit substantially from four or six months of concentrated research.

English and Italian Language Requirements

Applicants must be:

  • Conversant in English, and
  • Familiar with Italian.

The language requirement is important because the fellowship is based at an Italian Renaissance research center in Florence and involves engagement with Italian scholarly resources and the wider academic community.

Research Must Be Feasible in Florence

Applicants must demonstrate that it is possible to conduct most of their research in Florence.

This does not necessarily mean that every source required for the project must be located in Florence.

Rather, the proposed research should be sufficiently connected to the resources available in Florence to justify a residential appointment at I Tatti.

Applicants should therefore carefully consider the research materials, archives, libraries, collections, and scholarly resources they will need during the fellowship.

Priority for Early- and Mid-Career Scholars

The fellowship gives priority to early- and mid-career scholars.

This does not mean that senior scholars are necessarily excluded. Rather, the selection process gives particular consideration to applicants at earlier and middle stages of their academic careers.

Candidates should therefore explain clearly how the fellowship would contribute to the development and advancement of their research.

Global Eligibility: Scholars From All Nations Can Apply

The Berenson Fellowship welcomes applications from scholars from all nations.

There is no stated restriction limiting applications to a particular country, nationality, continent, or racial group.

The fellowship specifically gives special consideration to candidates who do not have regular access to research materials and facilities in Italy.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to scholars based outside Italy who would significantly benefit from spending an extended research period at I Tatti.

Who Can Apply?

In general, the opportunity is aimed at:

  • Scholars who already hold a PhD.
  • Researchers working in relevant Renaissance and early modern fields.
  • Early-career scholars.
  • Mid-career scholars.
  • Scholars researching transnational relationships involving Italy.
  • Researchers working in architecture and the arts.
  • Historians.
  • Philosophers.
  • Literature scholars.
  • Music scholars.
  • Historians of science.
  • Scholars whose projects can be substantially researched in Florence.
  • Researchers conversant in English and familiar with Italian.
  • Scholars from any country or nationality.

The fellowship is therefore international in scope, and scholars from Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, North America, Oceania, the Middle East, and other regions may apply, provided they meet the academic and research requirements.

Who Is Not Eligible?

Potential applicants should take note of several restrictions.

You may not qualify if:

  • You do not yet have a PhD at the time of application.
  • You are currently working toward a second PhD.
  • Your proposed project cannot be substantially researched in Florence.
  • You are unable to work in English and do not have familiarity with Italian.
  • You intend to use the fellowship period to work simultaneously on unrelated books or articles.
  • You plan to take on teaching or other professional obligations during the fellowship.
  • You have previously held a Term Fellowship at I Tatti, except if you previously held a Graduate Fellowship.
  • You have already used the fellowship opportunity in a way that conflicts with the Term Fellowship’s one-time restriction.

Applicants should carefully review the official application requirements before submitting their application.

Previous I Tatti Appointments and One-Time Fellowship Rule

Term Fellowships at I Tatti can be held only once.

They also cannot be deferred.

The fellowship is intended for scholars who have not previously held appointments at I Tatti, with the exception of Graduate Fellows.

This means previous affiliation with I Tatti is an important factor to consider before applying.

Restrictions During the Fellowship

The residential fellowship comes with several obligations and restrictions.

No Teaching Positions

Fellows may not take on other obligations such as teaching positions, including part-time teaching, during any part of the fellowship period.

Applicants who currently teach should therefore consider whether they can fully comply with this requirement.

No Simultaneous Fellowship or Award

The Berenson Fellowship may not be held concurrently with another fellowship or award.

Applicants who receive external funding should carefully consider whether it can be held alongside the I Tatti fellowship.

Outside Grants and Salary

If an applicant receives a partial salary or outside grant, this information must be disclosed either:

  • In the application, or
  • In subsequent correspondence with the Director.

Permission must also be received where required.

Applicants should therefore be transparent about other sources of financial support.

Visa and Health Insurance Responsibilities

International Fellows are responsible for handling their own immigration and health-related arrangements.

The Fellow is responsible for obtaining:

  • A visa, where required.
  • A permesso di soggiorno where applicable.
  • Health coverage.
  • Appropriate documentation for accompanying family members, where relevant.

Applicants must determine whether they require a visa and, if one is necessary, obtain it before travelling.

Prospective international applicants should therefore begin investigating Italian immigration requirements well before the fellowship start date.

Application Process for the Berenson Fellowship

Applications are submitted electronically.

Applicants can prepare their application in either:

  • English, or
  • Italian.

Candidates should ensure that all required application materials are completed and submitted through the designated online application system.

The application should present a compelling research project and demonstrate the applicant’s scholarly ability and potential contribution to I Tatti’s intellectual community.

What Makes a Strong Application?

Although selection is competitive, several elements are explicitly important in the evaluation process.

The selection committee pays particular attention to:

  1. The strength of the proposed project
  2. The potential of the project to produce original results
  3. The candidate’s curriculum vitae
  4. The candidate’s ability to contribute collegially to I Tatti’s intellectual life

Applicants should therefore avoid treating the application as simply a funding request.

Instead, the application should demonstrate:

  • A clearly defined research question.
  • A strong understanding of existing scholarship.
  • A convincing explanation of the project’s originality.
  • A realistic research plan.
  • A strong connection to the “Italy in the World” theme.
  • A clear reason why Florence and I Tatti are important for the research.
  • Evidence of the applicant’s scholarly achievements.
  • The potential significance of the expected results.

Letters of Recommendation

Applicants must arrange for two scholars who know their work well to submit recommendations online.

The recommendation letters may be written in:

  • English, or
  • Italian.

The referees must submit their recommendations electronically by:

November 21, 2026

Applicants are strongly encouraged to register their referees early through the reference section of the application system.

Once registered, referees will receive an email explaining how to access the system and submit their recommendations.

Applicants are responsible for informing their referees about:

  • The nature of the proposed research project.
  • The fellowship being applied for.
  • The application deadline.
  • The separate recommendation deadline.

Giving referees adequate notice can help ensure that recommendations are submitted on time.

Berenson Fellowship Deadlines

There are two important dates applicants should remember.

Main Application Deadline

November 16, 2026

Applications must be submitted electronically by midnight Cambridge, Massachusetts time on November 16, 2026.

Recommendation Letter Deadline

November 21, 2026

The two required recommendation letters must be submitted online by November 21, 2026.

Because the recommendation deadline comes after the main application deadline, applicants should not wait until the last minute to register their referees.

Important Application Restriction

Scholars may apply for only one type of I Tatti Fellowship per academic year.

Applicants considering multiple I Tatti fellowship categories should therefore carefully determine which fellowship best matches their research and career circumstances before submitting an application.

How to Prepare a Competitive Application

Applicants interested in the Berenson Fellowship should approach the application strategically.

1. Develop a Clearly Defined Research Project

Your project should have a clear research question and demonstrate why the subject matters.

Avoid presenting a project that is too broad to complete meaningful work on during a four- or six-month residential fellowship.

2. Demonstrate the Transnational Dimension

Because the fellowship focuses on “Italy in the World,” applicants should make the international or cross-cultural dimension of their research clear.

Explain how the project examines relationships between Italy and another culture, region, society, intellectual tradition, or geographical area.

3. Explain Why Florence Matters

A strong application should establish why conducting research at I Tatti and in Florence is important.

Applicants should identify the resources, collections, scholarly environment, or research networks that make Florence particularly valuable for the project.

4. Emphasize Originality

The selection committee specifically considers the potential of the proposed project to produce original results.

Applicants should clearly explain what their research contributes that existing scholarship does not adequately address.

5. Present a Strong CV

The curriculum vitae is an important component of the evaluation.

Applicants should clearly present relevant:

  • Academic qualifications.
  • Publications.
  • Research experience.
  • Previous scholarly achievements.
  • Fellowships and awards.
  • Relevant academic positions.
  • Conference participation.
  • Other evidence of research ability.

6. Choose Appropriate Referees

The two recommenders should know the applicant’s scholarly work well enough to provide meaningful assessments.

Applicants should give referees sufficient information about the proposed project so that their recommendations can address the candidate’s research ability and potential.

APPLY HERE

Why Scholars From Outside Italy May Find This Fellowship Particularly Valuable

The fellowship explicitly gives special consideration to candidates without regular access to research materials and facilities in Italy.

This can be particularly significant for scholars based in countries where access to Italian Renaissance collections, archives, libraries, and specialized academic networks is limited.

For researchers from Africa, Asia, Latin America, and other regions, the fellowship may provide an opportunity to access resources and develop scholarly relationships that would otherwise be difficult to obtain.

The international character of the fellowship also fits the broader goal of encouraging geographically expansive approaches to Renaissance studies.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Berenson Fellowship 2027–2028 at Harvard University’s I Tatti.

Residential Nature of the Fellowship

The Berenson Fellowship is not a remote fellowship.

Successful Fellows must live in the Florence area and spend at least three days per week at I Tatti.

Applicants should therefore be prepared for an extended period of residence in Italy.

The residential requirement is central to the fellowship because I Tatti seeks to foster direct scholarly interaction among researchers.

Applicants should consider accommodation, visa requirements, health coverage, travel, and other relocation arrangements when planning their application.

The Broader Academic Value of the Fellowship

Beyond the financial grant, the Berenson Fellowship can offer significant professional and intellectual value.

Researchers have the opportunity to work in an environment specifically dedicated to Italian Renaissance studies while engaging with scholars from different academic backgrounds.

The fellowship can support:

  • Concentrated research.
  • Development of original scholarship.
  • Access to specialized library resources.
  • International academic networking.
  • Interdisciplinary collaboration.
  • Exposure to different approaches to Renaissance studies.
  • Development of manuscripts and other scholarly outputs.
  • Deeper engagement with Italian research resources.
  • Participation in an international scholarly community.

For scholars whose projects require sustained concentration and access to specialized resources, this environment can be particularly valuable.
